newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel seeks foreign money for transport projects.
newsitem.headline: Israel seeks foreign money for transport projects.

text.p: Israeli Transport Minister Yitzhak Levy will travel to New York this week with a briefcase full of infrastructure projects estimated at $20 billion in which he hopes to interest foreign investors.

Levy said on Sunday the government hoped the private sector would ultimately finance 25 percent of the planned projects, which include inter-city highways, urban roads, railways and major airport and port expansions. Most of them due to be completed by the year 2010.

He expressed little concern about the impact of the recent clashes between Israelis and Palestinians that have raised doubts about the future of Middle East peace. "All the plans are founded on the basic assumption that there will be peace," he told a news conference.
"It doesn't make a difference which government is in power," he said. "Anyone who thinks that even if there is an agreement on Hebron...there won't be another blow-up in another year is mistaken."
A long-delayed Israeli pullback from parts of the West Bank town of Hebron is expected to be one of the central issues at Palestinian-Israeli talks scheduled for Sunday.
Levy, a member of the right-wing National Religious Party, said expanding port capacity was based on the assumption that neighbouring Jordan would be shipping cargo through Israel.
The Palestinian Authority, he said, would not undertake any major port construction of its own for years to come and would therefore also rely on Israel.

The principal projects Levy will be proposing to foreign investors are for the greater Tel Aviv area, where plans call for $5 billion to be invested. Most of it will be for a network of suburban, urban and light railways.
The second major project is a $1.5 billion expansion of Ben- Gurion International Airport outside Tel Aviv. The third is $1.5 billion for expanding Haifa and Ashdod ports.
Levy said the government had not decided how to integrate private sector investment into the projects.

He cited figures showing that even after increasing transport-infrastructure investment to $800 million in 1995 from about $300 million annually in the early 1990s, Israel had not caught up with its needs.
Current development plans are based on gross domestic product (GDP) expanding 94 percent to $165 billion by 2010 and per capita GDP increasing 56 percent to $25,000.

The minister said he would stop in London on his return from New York to study the privatisation of British Airways. Although he noted the airline was successfully floated, he said that did not indicate that Israel planned to take its state-owned carrier El AL public too.
The minister will meet investors at the Israel-North America Business Conference on October 8 to 10 in New York.
